prompt:
Write a technical description of about 800 words of how Git stores a commit, covering blobs, trees, commit objects and refs. The reader is a developer who uses Git every day and has never looked inside the .git directory.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
When you run git commit, Git does not record a list of changes. It records a snapshot of the whole project, built from four kinds of plain data in the .git directory: blobs, trees, commit objects and refs. The first three live in a content-addressed store under .git/objects, and the fourth is a set of small text files that give names to some of them. Once you see how these fit together, most of Git's everyday behaviour stops being mysterious.

Start with the object store. Every object is named by a SHA-1 hash, 40 hexadecimal characters long, which Git calculates from the object's type, its size and its content. Newer repositories can be created with SHA-256 instead, giving 64 characters, but the structure is the same. A loose object is stored as a file whose directory is the first two characters of the hash and whose filename is the remaining 38. The empty file has the hash e69de29bb2d1d6434b8b29ae775ad8c2e48c5391, so its object sits at .git/objects/e6/9de29bb2d1d6434b8b29ae775ad8c2e48c5391. The file is compressed with zlib. Once decompressed it begins with the type, a space, the size in bytes and a null byte, and the content follows. Because the name comes from the content, an object can never change. If the content changes, the result is a different object with a different name.

A blob holds the contents of one file and nothing else. It has no filename, no permissions and no timestamp. Two files with identical contents, in different directories or at different points in history, share a single blob. If you change one line in a large file, Git writes a new blob for the whole of the new version. It does not store the difference at this stage. You can check this yourself with git hash-object, which prints the hash a file would have, and git cat-file -p, which prints the content of any object when given its hash.

The names and the directory structure live in trees. A tree is a list of entries, and each entry has a mode, a name and the hash of another object. The mode says what kind of thing the entry is: 100644 for an ordinary file, 100755 for an executable, 120000 for a symbolic link, and 40000 for a subdirectory. An entry for a file points to a blob. An entry for a subdirectory points to another tree. A project with a src directory therefore has a root tree that lists README.md as a blob and src as a tree, and the src tree lists its own files in turn. The hash of the root tree depends on everything beneath it, so it identifies the exact state of every file in the project. If one file deep in the structure changes, its blob gets a new hash, the tree that contains it gets a new hash, and so does every tree above it up to the root. Trees that were not touched keep their old hashes and are reused.

A commit object is a short piece of text. It has a line giving the hash of the root tree, then one line for each parent commit, then an author line and a committer line, each with a name, an email address, a Unix timestamp and a timezone offset. A blank line follows, and then the message exactly as you wrote it. The first commit in a repository has no parent, an ordinary commit has one, and a merge commit has two or more. The commit does not contain any file data itself. It points to a tree, and the tree points to the blobs. History is the chain formed by the parent lines, and because each commit's hash covers its parent's hash, changing any old commit would change the hash of every commit after it. This is why amending or rebasing produces new commits and leaves the originals where they were until Git later discards them as unreachable.

Objects are found by hash, and nobody wants to remember hashes, so refs supply the names. A branch is a file under .git/refs/heads whose entire content is the 40-character hash of a commit followed by a newline. The file .git/refs/heads/main is the branch main. Tags are kept in the same way under .git/refs/tags, and remote-tracking branches under .git/refs/remotes. Creating a branch writes 41 bytes to a file, which is why it is so fast. Committing on a branch writes the new commit and then replaces the hash in that branch's file. A file called HEAD in the .git directory records where you currently are. Usually it holds a line such as ref: refs/heads/main, pointing at a branch. When you check out a commit directly, it holds a bare hash instead, which is what Git means by a detached HEAD. In larger repositories many refs are gathered into a single .git/packed-refs file for efficiency, but the meaning is the same.

Putting this together, a commit goes as follows. Staging a file with git add writes its blob into the object store and records the hash, name and mode in .git/index. Running git commit turns the index into a set of tree objects, writes a commit object that names the new root tree and the current commit as its parent, and moves the current branch's ref to the new commit. Nothing already in the store is altered. Over time loose objects pile up, and git gc gathers them into packfiles, where similar objects are stored as deltas against one another. This is where the space saving happens, and it is a storage detail only. The model you see through git cat-file stays the same: blobs, trees, commits and refs.
